style_when: the article describes one decisive moment or place — a yard at dawn, a control room, a shutdown line, a handover — that a film still could hold
prompt: Anamorphic 35mm cinematic film still, wide low-angle establishing shot at blue hour: a high-voltage substation under construction on a gravel yard, its galvanised steel lattice gantry and stacked porcelain insulators rising off-centre on the left third, copper busbars lacing between steel posts, a transformer waiting wrapped in shipping tarp on its poured concrete pad, a mobile crane silhouetted behind, string-lined foundation outlines in the gravel. A vast teal dusk sky and a dark unfinished data hall shell fill the right of the frame as negative space. One amber worklight rakes across the yard from the left, deep shadows, steel blue, graphite and weathered orange palette, crisp atmospheric depth, fine film grain, no people, no logos.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, legible signage, watermarks
rationale: The story turns on one place and one timeline — the substation a team must start paying for now and wait on for four-plus years — so a wide cinematic establishing shot carries the scale and the wait better than any close-up or constructed render. Blue-hour worklight on active construction beside a dark data hall shell states the sequencing conflict — power built before the building — with no invented apparatus.
subject: a high-voltage substation under construction beside a dark, unfinished data hall shell
core_thesis: The median wait from grid-queue request to a live power feed has doubled past four years — 55 months for feeds over 200 megawatts — so the substation commitment is a five-year capital bet placed at project start, not a detail settled when the racks are ordered.
core_conflict: The multi-year interconnection queue versus the hardware build schedule: capital must be committed years before the feed (or the 77% drop-out) is known, and no reform clears the wait.
composition: Low-angle extreme asymmetry: the substation commanding the left third of the frame, vast dusk sky and the dark data hall shell filling the right as editorial negative space.
